titleEn: Restore us, and we shall be saved
progression: | Em Em | C C | Am B7 | Em Em |
intro: A national lament built around one refrain said three times, at verses 4, 8 and 20: restore us, light up Your face, and we are saved. Watch the divine name in front of it grow each time, from God, to God of hosts, to LORD God of hosts, while the request itself never changes a word. Between the second and third refrain the psalm stops speaking plainly and tells the story of a vine brought out of Egypt, planted, spread to the sea, and then left with its walls broken so that anyone passing can help themselves. It is said in many communities on fast days and at times of public trouble. For a learner it is the best short lesson in the possessive suffix on a feminine noun: from verse 9 to verse 13 almost every second word ends in her.

stichs.en: For the leader; on Lilies. A testimony.
Of Asaph, a psalm.

verses.summary: A musical direction whose meaning is no longer recoverable, followed by the word testimony, which is the one term in the heading that also belongs to the psalm's subject.

stichs.en: Shepherd of Israel, listen,
You who drive Joseph like a flock,
enthroned on the cherubim, shine out.

verses.summary: Two images of God stacked in one verse, a herdsman on foot and a king on a throne. The verb at the end belongs to light breaking out, and it sets up the refrain about a face that shines.

stichs.en: In front of Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh,
wake up Your strength,
and come to save us.

verses.summary: Three tribes and no others. They are the descendants of Rachel, and in the wilderness camp they march together on the same side of the ark, which is why they are the tribes God would be walking in front of.

stichs.en: God, bring us back,
and light up Your face, and we are saved.

verses.summary: The refrain in its shortest form. Note the causative verb {{4.1}}: the people do not ask to return, they ask to be returned, and the salvation at the end is passive too.

stichs.en: LORD God of hosts,
how long will You smoulder at Your people's prayer?

verses.summary: The complaint is sharper than it looks. It is not that prayer goes unanswered but that praying is itself what draws the anger, which makes the psalm a prayer that admits it may make things worse.

stichs.en: You have fed them bread made of tears,
and given them tears to drink by the measure.

glosses: and You gave them to drink
verses.summary: Grief served as rations, in the two forms a host provides, solid and liquid. The last word is a unit of volume, so the weeping is being issued rather than merely suffered.

stichs.en: You make us something our neighbours fight over,
and our enemies mock us as they please.

verses.summary: The subject of the damaging verb is still You. Throughout this section the enemies are instruments and God is the agent, which is what gives the refrain something to ask for.

stichs.en: God of hosts, bring us back,
and light up Your face, and we are saved.

verses.summary: Second time, and the only change is one word added to the name. The request is held fixed on purpose while the address to God escalates.

stichs.en: A vine You pulled up out of Egypt;
You drove out nations and planted it.

verses.summary: The allegory begins without announcing itself. The verb of moving the vine is the one used for a camp striking tents and setting off, so the exodus is still being described, in a different register.

stichs.en: You cleared the ground in front of it,
and it rooted its roots
and filled the land.

verses.summary: God prepares and then stops acting; the vine takes over as the subject of the verbs. That handover is what makes the later damage feel like an interruption rather than a policy.

stichs.en: Mountains were covered by its shade,
and mighty cedars by its branches.

verses.summary: A vine covering cedars is a deliberate impossibility. The last two words can be read as cedars of God or as divine cedars, and either way the plant has outgrown the scale of a plant.

stichs.en: It sent its branches out as far as the Sea,
and its shoots to the River.

verses.summary: The two borders of the promised territory, west and east, given as the reach of a plant rather than as a map. This is the high point, and the next word is why.

stichs.en: Why have You broken down its walls,
so that everyone passing on the road picks at it?

verses.summary: The hinge of the whole psalm, and it is a question rather than an accusation. What was removed is not the vine but its fence, so the ruin comes from being left open, not from being attacked.

stichs.en: A boar out of the forest chews it up,
and whatever moves in the field grazes on it.

verses.summary: One named animal and one unnamed thing. The vagueness of {{14.3}} does more work than the boar does: the vineyard is now open to anything at all.

stichs.en: God of hosts, come back, please:
look down from heaven and see,
and take account of this vine,

verses.summary: The plea turns the refrain's verb around: instead of bring us back, it says come back Yourself. The demonstrative at the end points at the vine as if the two of them were standing in the ruined field.

stichs.en: and the stock Your own right hand planted,
and upon the son You raised strong for Yourself.

verses.summary: The Hebrew of the second half is difficult and the reading is disputed: the same phrase turns up again at the end of verse 18, and some hold that it was copied in here by accident while others read it as deliberate, the branch of the vine and the son of the people named by one word.

stichs.en: Burned with fire, cut back,
at the blast of Your face they are lost.

verses.summary: The face returns, and here it destroys. The refrain asks for that same face to shine instead, so the psalm is asking for a change in the direction of one thing, not for a different God.

stichs.en: Let Your hand rest on the man at Your right hand,
on the son of man You raised strong for Yourself.

verses.summary: The allegory drops and a person appears, unnamed. Whoever this is, the psalm asks for the hand that broke the walls to be placed on him instead.

stichs.en: Then we will not turn away from You;
keep us alive, and we will call on Your name.

verses.summary: The only promise in the psalm, and it is carefully ordered: life first, calling on the name second. Nothing is offered in advance.

stichs.en: LORD God of hosts, bring us back,
light up Your face, and we are saved.

verses.summary: Third and last, with the full name at the front and the conjunction dropped from the middle. The psalm ends on the request it started with and never reports an answer.

pardes.body: The spine is the refrain at verses 4, 8 and 20. Its words do not change; the name in front of it does, going from God, to God of hosts, to {{20.0}} with the full name, so the psalm gets louder by addressing rather than by asking for more. Between the refrains are two blocks. The first, verses 5 to 7, is plain complaint with God as the subject of every damaging verb. The second, verses 9 to 18, is an allegory of a vine, and it runs a complete arc: transplanted from Egypt, given cleared ground, grown past all proportion to the sea and the River, then left unfenced and eaten. The question at verse 13 is the turn. Nothing in the psalm reports that the request was granted.

Three details worth stopping on. First, {{1.2}} in the heading is either the name of a melody or the word for lilies, and no one now knows which; the following word, testimony, is a legal term, so the heading pairs a flower with a courtroom. Second, the tribes of verse 3 are Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, the sons and grandsons of Rachel, and in the wilderness camp of the book of Numbers they travel together on the west side, which is why they and no others are the tribes God is asked to walk in front of. Joseph in verse 2 stands for the same group. Third, the hardest words in the psalm are the end of verse 16. The phrase there matches the end of verse 18 almost exactly, and {{16.5}} against {{18.6}} is a son in both cases, but in verse 16 the surrounding words are about a plant. Whether verse 16 is an accidental duplication or a deliberate pun on a shoot and a son is disputed, and the difficulty is old enough that ancient translations already disagree with one another here.

The vine is the standing image for Israel in the prophets, and this psalm is the version told from inside, as a complaint rather than a verdict: elsewhere the vineyard is torn down because it produced bad fruit, and here no fault at all is named, only walls that were removed. Reading the two together is what generates the traditional question the psalm invites, which is whether the exile is punishment or abandonment, and the psalm answers by refusing to say. The man of the right hand in verse 18 has been read as the king, as the people personified, and in later tradition messianically, since a son of man raised strong for God is exactly the figure such readings look for. The three occurrences of the refrain have also been counted as three exiles, with the escalating name marking how much further away the speaker feels each time.

The whole psalm turns on the face. The refrain asks for {{4.2}}, make Your face shine, and verse 17 shows the same face turned the other way, where its blast destroys. This is the language of the priestly blessing, where the LORD makes His face shine on you, so the congregation is asking to be put back inside a blessing they already know the words of. In the mystical reading the hiding of the face is not absence but concealment: the light is undiminished and the vine is unwatched only from below. That is why the request is never for a new gift but for a return of the same one, and why the refrain has to be said three times without changing, since what changes is the one saying it. The vine, rooted downward and spreading to the two waters, is read in the same tradition as the shape by which what is above gets planted below and is expected to fill the land.
